screens.title: Inverse Kinematics (IK) for Dynamic Animation
screens.subtitle: Make characters reach, step, and look naturally at runtime using Unity's IK features

narration.text: Welcome. In this chapter you will learn how inverse kinematics lets a character's hand, foot, or head meet a world-space target without manually rotating every joint. We begin by contrasting forward kinematics, the animator's traditional keyframe approach, with inverse kinematics, which solves joint rotations from a desired end effector position. You will see how Unity's Mecanim system exposes IK hooks and an OnAnimatorIK callback that runs after animations are evaluated, giving you a deterministic place to override final poses. We'll walk through a practical C# example that drives a right-hand target and an elbow hint, and you will learn how to blend IK weights to avoid abrupt motion. Finally, we'll cover common mistakes—such as calling IK methods outside the correct callback or forgetting to set weights—and performance tradeoffs when driving many limbs at high frequency. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to set up a simple IK rig, connect a target and hint, and write a script that makes a character reach for a moving sphere in a stable, playable way.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: IK lets you specify an end effector position and have joint rotations computed automatically, enabling dynamic, interactive poses in gameplay.

narration.text: Over the next screens you'll develop four verified competencies. Second, you'll know how to configure a humanoid rig in Unity so Mecanim's IK features are available and reliable. Third, you'll implement a C# controller that uses the OnAnimatorIK callback to set IK position, rotation, weights, and optional hints for limbs. Fourth, you'll apply IK to procedural effects such as a look-at behavior or ground-adaptive foot placement. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with a practical milestone: inspect an Animator, wire a target and hint in the Inspector, write and test a small script that toggles ikWeight, and observe how blending weights avoids animation conflicts. screens.title: Forward Kinematics vs Inverse Kinematics
screens.subtitle: Why IK is preferable for runtime targeting

narration.text: Start by holding a simple mental model: forward kinematics is the animator's workflow—set rotations for each joint and the chain follows. It is perfect for authored clips and keyframes, but it is not suited to procedural demands where you need a fingertip to meet a moving object. Inverse kinematics flips the problem. Instead of setting elbow and shoulder rotations and hoping the hand ends up on the target, you specify the desired hand position and the IK solver computes the joint rotations required. This matters in games because targets move and the world is unpredictable. A concrete example: if a rolling ball approaches a character, FK would require manually animating the arm to match the ball, whereas IK allows the runtime code to move the hand to the ball's position immediately. A common misconception is that IK removes the need for artist input; in reality, good IK setups still need correct rigging, reasonable targets, and hints to produce natural bends. Takeaway: use FK for authored, predictable motion, and use IK when you need runtime, world-space accuracy for end effectors. Which parts of your system require precise contact will determine where to add IK.

keyIdea.title: Comparison takeaway
keyIdea.text: Use FK for authored animations and IK for precise, procedural positioning of end effectors during gameplay.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › FK vs IK
Forward Kinematics (FK)

Rotate joints sequentially; animator sets each joint transform. Great for authored motion, limited for reactive tasks.

Example: keyframe shoulder, then elbow, then wrist to create a wave animation.
Misconception: FK is not obsolete; it's the basis for many base clips that IK will augment.
Key Takeaway

FK gives you precise authored motion, but not runtime adaptability for reaching targets.

Inverse Kinematics (IK)

Provide a desired end effector position and rotation; the solver computes joint rotations to meet that target. Ideal for runtime interaction and adaptive animation.

Concrete: set the right-hand world position to a moving sphere and the solver bends the shoulder and elbow automatically.
Misconception: IK doesn't always produce perfect results without hints and reasonable targets.
Pro Tip

Blend IK weights and use hints to keep solver output natural and avoid fighting base animation.

screens.title: Where to Apply IK in Unity's Animation Pipeline
screens.subtitle: OnAnimatorIK and the Animator evaluation order

narration.text: To apply IK reliably you must place your code in the right phase of Unity's animation pipeline. Unity evaluates Animator layers and base animation first, then calls OnAnimatorIK before final pose application. This callback is the correct place to override joint transforms via the Animator A P I. Practically, this means your script obtains a reference to the Animator, implements OnAnimatorIK, and inside that function calls SetIKPosition, SetIKRotation, and SetIKPositionWeight for the goals you intend to override. This separation prevents conflicts where your script runs too early or too late. A concrete scenario: if you set IK targets in Update, the Animator will overwrite those changes during its evaluation, so the hand will not reach the target. A common mistake is forgetting to get the Animator reference; the callback will still execute, but null checks must guard calls. Another practical tip is to consider root motion: if Apply Root Motion is enabled, the Animator may move the character's transform; IK adjusts joints relative to that final root pose. Final takeaway: OnAnimatorIK is the single, reliable hook for setting IK each frame so the Animator applies your overrides coherently.

keyIdea.title: Pipeline rule
keyIdea.text: Always set IK inside OnAnimatorIK so the Animator integrates your overrides after evaluating base animation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › OnAnimatorIK Architecture
Animation Evaluation Flow
1. Animator evaluates states and blends, producing a base pose.
2. Unity calls OnAnimatorIK on MonoBehaviours attached to the same GameObject so you can apply IK overrides.
3. The final pose, including your IK adjustments, is applied to the skeleton and rendered.
// Example skeleton for OnAnimatorIK
void OnAnimatorIK(int layerIndex)
{
    if (animator == null) return;
    // Set IK weights and positions here so the Animator applies them
}
Explanation
  • • Placing IK calls in Update will not be applied correctly.
  • • Null-check your Animator reference to avoid runtime errors.
  • • Consider root motion: IK offsets are applied to the final skeleton after root movement.
Common Mistake

Calling SetIKPosition outside OnAnimatorIK results in no visible IK effect.

screens.title: Key IK Methods in the Animator API
screens.subtitle: SetIKPosition, SetIKRotation, SetLookAt and weights

narration.text: Let's walk through the Animator A P I methods you will use when applying IK. The most important are SetIKPosition and SetIKRotation, which assign a world-space target for an AvatarIKGoal such as RightHand or LeftFoot. Each goal must also have its position and rotation weights set using SetIKPositionWeight and SetIKRotationWeight; a weight of zero disables IK influence while one enables full control. For gaze control use SetLookAtPosition and SetLookAtWeight to influence body, head, and eyes. A practical example is making a character look at a moving object: set the look-at weight with body, head, and eyes components, then call SetLookAtPosition with the target's world position. Remember to check for null targets and to zero weights when the target is absent. A common misconception is that a weight alone is sufficient; you must call both the SetIKPosition and the weight setter so the Animator knows to apply the target. Finally, use hint setters like SetIKHintPosition for elbows and knees to nudge the solver toward natural joint bends. These methods are lightweight individually, but excessive simultaneous IK on many limbs can affect performance, so profile when necessary.

keyIdea.title: API essentials
keyIdea.text: Use SetIKPosition/Rotation and matching weight setters inside OnAnimatorIK; use SetLookAt for gaze and hints for natural bends.

Common IK calls
animator.SetIKPosition(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, target.position);
animator.SetIKRotation(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, target.rotation);
animator.SetIKPositionWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, ikWeight);
animator.SetIKRotationWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, ikWeight);

animator.SetLookAtWeight(weight, body, head, eyes, clamp);
animator.SetLookAtPosition(lookAtTarget.position);
Note: always set weights to control influence. For hints use SetIKHintPosition and SetIKHintPositionWeight to improve elbow and knee solutions.
Explanation
  • • Set the world-space target before the Animator applies the final pose.
  • • Weights blend the solver output with base animation to avoid abrupt changes.
  • • Hints guide the solver to choose a natural joint bend direction.
Common Mistake

Not setting weights or calling the methods outside OnAnimatorIK causes no visible IK effect.

screens.title: HandIKController — Practical C# Example
screens.subtitle: Implementing OnAnimatorIK to drive a right-hand target

narration.text: Now let's inspect a practical script pattern that you will implement and test. The HandIKController holds references to an Animator, a right-hand target transform, and an elbow hint transform. The script exposes a float ikWeight that you change to blend IK influence. At Start the Animator reference is acquired if not assigned in the Inspector. The OnAnimatorIK callback checks for the animator and target, sets position and rotation weights, assigns the target position and rotation, and optionally sets the hint position and its weight. If the target is null, the script zeroes the weights so the base animation plays unmodified. A live test: attach the script to the humanoid, drag the target sphere and elbow hint into the fields, run Play, and move the sphere. Increase ikWeight from zero to one to watch the hand follow. A common misconception is to treat ikWeight as a toggle only; instead, animate it smoothly to avoid sudden snapping between animation and IK. This example is the core you will reuse for feet, look-at, or any other end effector. In practical terms, implementing onanimatorik to drive a right-hand target. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Script pattern
keyIdea.text: A simple component exposes Animator and target references, applies IK inside OnAnimatorIK, and blends influence via ikWeight.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › HandIKController
Starter Script (visual)
public class HandIKController : MonoBehaviour
{
    public Animator animator;
    public Transform ikTargetSphere;
    public Transform elbowHint;
    [Range(0,1)] public float ikWeight = 0f;

    void Start()
    {
        if (animator == null) animator = GetComponent();
    }

    void OnAnimatorIK(int layerIndex)
    {
        if (animator == null) return;
        animator.SetIKPositionWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, ikWeight);
        animator.SetIKRotationWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, ikWeight);
        if (ikTargetSphere != null) {
            animator.SetIKPosition(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, ikTargetSphere.position);
            animator.SetIKRotation(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, ikTargetSphere.rotation);
            if (elbowHint != null) {
                animator.SetIKHintPositionWeight(AvatarIKHint.RightElbow, ikWeight);
                animator.SetIKHintPosition(AvatarIKHint.RightElbow, elbowHint.position);
            }
        } else {
            animator.SetIKPositionWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, 0);
            animator.SetIKRotationWeight(AvatarIKGoal.RightHand, 0);
        }
    }
}
Runtime checklist
  • • Animator reference is not null and Avatar is Humanoid.
  • • Target and hint transforms are assigned in the Inspector.
  • • ikWeight is animated or adjusted in Play to observe blending.
  • • Zero weights when target is removed to prevent residual overrides.
Try This

Animate ikWeight from 0 to 1 over half a second to observe a smooth transition between base animation and IK.

screens.title: Inspector and Scene Setup
screens.subtitle: Place targets, hints, and configure the Animator

narration.text: A clean scene and Inspector setup make testing IK straightforward. First, import or use a humanoid character with a Humanoid avatar. Add an Animator component and assign a simple Animator Controller that plays an idle animation so the skeleton has a base pose. Create a sphere named IKTargetSphere and position it near the expected reach of the right hand, slightly outside reach to see the solver move the arm. Create an empty GameObject named RightElbowHint and place it behind the elbow to encourage a natural bend toward the back when reaching. Attach the HandIKController to the character and drag the sphere and hint into their respective fields in the Inspector. If the Animator uses root motion, decide whether Apply Root Motion should be checked—root motion can be useful but remember IK is applied after the root transforms. Finally, run Play and adjust ikWeight in the Inspector; if the hand snaps or contorts, move the hint or adjust the target distance. A common misconception is to stack multiple overlapping targets on the same limb; prefer one clear target per end effector and use hints sparingly to guide the solver.

keyIdea.title: Setup rule
keyIdea.text: Position one target per end effector and place hints to guide elbow and knee bends; test weight blending in Play mode.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Inspector & Scene Setup
Step-by-step
  1. 1. Assign a Humanoid avatar and Animator component with an idle state.
  2. 2. Create IKTargetSphere and position it within reachable range of the right hand.
  3. 3. Create RightElbowHint slightly behind the elbow to guide the bend direction.
  4. 4. Attach HandIKController to character and drag references into the Inspector.
  5. 5. Run Play and adjust ikWeight to observe blending.
Common adjustments
If elbow collapses inward, move the hint further behind or to the side.
If hand overshoots, reduce the distance between target and shoulder or lower ikWeight.
If jitter occurs, smooth the target motion or tween the ikWeight instead of snapping.
Why it matters

A correct scene setup avoids solver artifacts and gives you repeatable, editable IK behavior during testing.

screens.title: Blending IK Weights and Avoiding Animation Fights
screens.subtitle: Smoothly combining authored clips with IK overrides

narration.text: Blending is central to making IK feel natural. IK weight controls how much the solver overrides the base animation. If you abruptly set the weight from zero to one, you can see pops where the hand snaps to the target. Instead, animate the weight over a short time window or lerp it in code to produce a smooth transition. A typical pattern is to increase ikWeight toward one when a target is within reach and decrease it when moving away. This also helps avoid fighting between complex authored hand animations and IK overrides. For example, if a base animation includes intricate hand motion, quickly applying full IK will cancel that detail; blending lets authored detail fade gracefully while IK assumes control. Another misconception is that higher weight always looks better. In many scenarios, a partial weight like 0.7 gives natural compromise between the animation and the solver, especially for small corrections. Finally, performance-wise, blend only the limbs that need IK and avoid setting weights on off-screen characters every frame when possible. The core takeaway: use weight blending as a creative control to preserve both animation quality and responsiveness.

keyIdea.title: Blend rule
keyIdea.text: Animate or lerp ikWeight to transition between base animation and IK smoothly; avoid snapping and unnecessary solver work.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Weight Blending
Blend pattern
// Example lerp in Update
float targetWeight = targetInRange ? 1f : 0f;
ikWeight = Mathf.MoveTowards(ikWeight, targetWeight, Time.deltaTime * 2f);
Use a time-based interpolation to move weight smoothly. Tune the speed to match animation timing and avoid visible pops.
Practical tips
  • • Only enable IK for limbs that must contact objects or follow dynamic targets.
  • • Gradually blend to maintain authored animation character and detail.
  • • Lower weight can produce subtle corrections rather than full overrides.
Misconception

Assuming ikWeight 1 is always best will often destroy subtle hand or foot animations; blend thoughtfully.

screens.title: IK Hints and End Effectors
screens.subtitle: Understanding hints, goals, and the end effector concept

narration.text: Two terms you will use constantly are end effector and hint. The end effector is the final node in a kinematic chain, usually a hand or foot. An IK Goal refers to that end effector within Mecanim, for example AvatarIKGoal. RightHand. A hint is an auxiliary world-space position that nudges the solver toward a desirable joint bend, such as an elbow pointing behind the arm when reaching forward. Hints are especially helpful when a limb could bend in multiple plausible directions; setting an elbow hint reduces twisting or inward collapse. Use hints sparingly and place them roughly in the expected bending direction relative to the joint. A concrete example: when a character reaches forward to grab a ledge, an elbow hint placed slightly behind and outside the shoulder encourages the elbow to fold naturally. A common error is positioning a hint too close to the joint or on the wrong side, which can worsen the solver result. The takeaway is simple: treat the end effector as your target and use a hint only when the solver needs directional guidance to produce a natural pose.

keyIdea.title: Hint usage
keyIdea.text: Hints guide the solver for natural joint bends; position them behind the joint in the expected bend direction.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › End Effector & Hints
Key terms
• End Effector: the limb tip you want to control, e.g. a hand or foot.
• IK Goal: Mecanim's identifier for an end effector, such as RightHand.
• Hint: an optional position guiding elbow or knee bending.
Concrete: place RightElbowHint slightly behind the elbow to encourage a natural fold when reaching forward.
Placement rules
  • • Place hints relative to joint orientation, not the target.
  • • Avoid placing hints too close to the joint to prevent erratic bending.
  • • Use hints when the solver has multiple valid bend solutions.
Quick Check

Move a hint and observe the elbow orientation; the hint should produce predictable, natural bend direction.

screens.title: Hands-on Lab: Make the Right Hand Reach for a Moving Sphere
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step implementation and testing plan

narration.text: Follow these steps to complete the hands-on lab from the chapter. First, import or use any humanoid model set to Humanoid. Assign an Animator and a simple controller with an idle clip. Create an IKTargetSphere and position it near but slightly out of reach of the character's right hand. Create a RightElbowHint behind the expected elbow direction. Add the HandIKController script to your character and wire Animator, IKTargetSphere, and RightElbowHint fields. Set ikWeight to zero to start. Enter Play mode and observe the base idle animation. Next, in the Inspector, slowly increase ikWeight toward one and watch the right hand move to the sphere. If you want dynamic movement, add the optional Update sample that oscillates the sphere's Y position using a sine function; this demonstrates how the hand follows moving targets. Troubleshoot by checking the Animator reference, ensuring weights are non-zero, and moving the hint if the elbow bends oddly. After you get it working, experiment with different ikWeight values to see how partial weights preserve hand animation detail while allowing contact. The final check is to ensure the motion is natural and stable across several cycles of the sphere movement.

keyIdea.text: Wire a target and hint, run Play, and adjust ikWeight so the hand reaches the moving sphere smoothly and naturally.

screens.title: Common IK Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.subtitle: Troubleshooting solver, weights, and callback issues

narration.text: When IK doesn't behave as expected, a few common causes account for most issues. First, calling SetIKPosition or weights outside OnAnimatorIK—such as in Update—will not affect the Animator's final pose. Always put those calls inside OnAnimatorIK. Second, zero weights: if position or rotation weights are zero, the IK has no influence. Ensure you set both SetIKPositionWeight and SetIKRotationWeight appropriately. Third, wrong AvatarIKGoal: make sure you target the correct limb; RightHand versus LeftHand are distinct choices. Fourth, missing Animator reference: null checks prevent silent failures; get the Animator component in Start if not assigned. Fifth, unrealistic targets: if the target is physically unreachable, the solver will produce unnatural poses; either move the target or use partial weights. Sixth, poor hint placement: placing hints too near joints or on the wrong side can cause twisted elbows or knees. Finally, conflicting complex animations: if the base clip moves the limb heavily, gradually blend IK or reduce weight during that animation. A simple checklist—callback, weights, goal, references, target reachability, hints, and blending—resolves most problems. Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Debugging IK
Top mistakes
  • • IK calls outside OnAnimatorIK.
  • • Position/rotation weights left at zero.
  • • Wrong AvatarIKGoal or missing Animator reference.
  • • Targets placed out of reach or hints mispositioned.
Fixes and checks
• Ensure OnAnimatorIK gets called and contains your SetIK calls.
• Set both position and rotation weights when you want full control.
• Test reachable targets and adjust hint placements to remove twisting.
• Blend weights to avoid fights with complex base animations.
Pro Tip

Log the Animator reference and IK weights during Play to quickly spot whether your code is executing and with what values.

screens.title: Advanced Uses: Look-At, Spine, and Feet on Slopes
screens.subtitle: Extending IK beyond hands and elbows

narration.text: IK goes beyond hands and feet. You can use SetLookAtPosition and SetLookAtWeight to make the head, eyes, and body orient toward a point of interest, adding immediate realism to character interactions. For foot placement on uneven ground, raycast from each foot to the terrain, compute a corrected world position, and apply SetIKPosition for AvatarIKGoal. LeftFoot and RightFoot inside OnAnimatorIK so their positions match the ground. For subtle spine or hip adjustments, use smaller weights applied to upper-body joints or mix in custom bone-level adjustments before applying IK. A practical example: when walking uphill, raycast to sample the slope at each foot and raise or rotate the foot to rest naturally on the surface; blend the weight based on contact confidence to avoid jitter. Performance is an important concern—limit per-frame heavy calculations, cache results when possible, and consider lowering solver frequency if necessary. The key idea is to combine targeted IK uses with careful blending and profiling to keep animations believable and runs efficient in gameplay. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Advanced IK
Patterns and examples
• Look-at: SetLookAtWeight and SetLookAtPosition to make the head and eyes track a moving object.
• Feet on slopes: raycast ground height and call SetIKPosition for each foot inside OnAnimatorIK.
• Spine tweaks: apply small weighted adjustments to upper-body joints for slope response.
Performance
  • • Limit the number of limbs updated each frame.
  • • Cache raycasts and reuse results within the frame.
  • • Tween weights instead of toggling to reduce solver instability.
Takeaway

Extend IK thoughtfully for gaze and grounding, and always profile to find tradeoffs between realism and runtime cost.

narration.text: Here are three concise ideas to keep front of mind. First, Forward Kinematics is joint-first animation—set rotations and the end effector follows. Second, Inverse Kinematics is target-first—give the solver a world-space endpoint and it computes joint rotations to reach it. Third, the OnAnimatorIK callback is the single correct place to call SetIKPosition, SetIKRotation, SetIKPositionWeight, SetIKRotationWeight, SetIKHintPosition, and SetLookAt methods so the Animator integrates your overrides after base animation evaluation. These three concepts form the backbone of practical IK work in Unity: understanding the difference, using the right A P I, and placing code in the right callback. Keep them in mind when designing interactions that require precise hand or foot placement or believable gaze behavior. narration.text: A short list of practical reminders to close the chapter. First, always set both the target and its weights—without weights the solver won't influence the limb. Second, use IK hints to guide elbows and knees when the solver has multiple valid solutions; place hints behind the joint in the expected bend direction. Third, test and blend: animate ikWeight or lerp it in code to create smooth transitions and avoid sudden snapping. Final takeaway: IK gives you powerful runtime control, but it is a tool to augment, not replace, authored animation; the best results come from combining quality base animations, careful hint placement, and thoughtful weight blending.
